say: Welcome back, data detectives! Newspapers, games and sports scores all come with averages. Today we find out what the average (mean) really is, how one number can trick it, and how a computer adds up a whole list in a blink.
Our rule today: work it out by hand first, then let the code test it. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
Quick-eye mean! I will show five numbers for five seconds only. No working out: just write your best guess of the mean. This is a guess, so any estimate is welcome. There are no points.
How did you guess so fast? Who looked for a number in the middle and checked that the big ones and small ones balance?
Before we add anything up: the mean number of letters in our names. Will it be bigger or smaller than the number of letters in YOUR name? Write a prediction.
If our tutor joins with a 30-letter name, will the mean go up a little or a lot? Thumbs up for a lot, sideways for a little.
stuck: Stuck on the hand calculation: add the values two at a time and write each running total, just like the variable total in the code.
Finished early: find a new value you could add that keeps the mean exactly the same. Test it in the program.

say: “Goals in 5 matches: 3, 0, 4, 1, 2. The 0 is a real value: that match counts. Total 3 + 0 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 10. Five matches, so the mean is 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Check by balancing: 3 is 1 above, 4 is 2 above: 3 above in all. 0 is 2 below, 1 is 1 below: 3 below in all. They balance, so 2 is right.”

“The mean of 4 test scores is 15, so the total must be 4 × 15 = 60. The three I know make 12 + 18 + 14 = 44. The missing score is 60 − 44 = 16. I never subtract from the mean: I subtract from the total.”

“Goals by 7 players: 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 25. The mean is 42 ÷ 7 = 6, but 6 of the 7 players scored fewer than 6! The one big value pulled the mean up. The median, the middle value in order, is 3. That describes a typical player better.”

do: Ask: “What is the total? How many values are there? Did you count the 0?”
Ask: “Before you calculate: will the mean go up, go down or stay the same? Why?”
Ask: “Point to the block that adds up. What is total after the second time round the loop?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find the total first. Mean × how many gives the total.”
Hint 2: “Draw the values as towers. Move cubes from tall towers to short ones until they are level.”
Hint 3: “For a trace table, do one loop at a time: which item? what is total now? then change i by 1.”

say: “Can the mean be a number that nobody in the group has?”
ask: “Can the mean be a number that nobody in the group has?”

Yes: the mean of 2 and 3 is 2.5, a number nobody in the group has. No: the mean is always between the smallest and the largest value. Levelling out moves cubes from taller towers to shorter ones, so the level can never be higher than the tallest tower or lower than the shortest.

say: “Today you found means by levelling and by dividing, worked backwards from a mean to a total, and caught a misleading average. And your code added up a whole list for you. Next lesson is our Showcase Challenge: start thinking about a puzzle you would like to turn into a program.”
Homework thought for next lesson: decide which starter you will change (A, B, C or Clock Jumper) and what your twist will be, so you can start building straight away.

p6l9-title.note: Objective: Find the mean as total ÷ number of values and as levelling out, use total = mean × number of values to find a missing value, predict how changing the data changes the mean, compare the mean with the median and mode when one value is extreme, and build a list program that adds up the data and finds the mean. Materials: Laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 (scratch.mit.edu; free, in the browser), starter file L9_Mean_Machine.sb3, workbook, pencil, mini whiteboard, about 25 linking cubes or counters for levelling towers. A calculator only for checking. Online: Data is collected in the chat. Children share their screen to show their code. The tutor shares the starter file L9_Mean_Machine.sb3 (one sprite with an empty list called data, total and i set up and an empty repeat; children use File, Load from your computer) or children build it from the slide in 5 minutes. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. The mean is familiar from primary school; the new parts are lists and loops, median and mode, and misleading averages. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5, warm-up 6.5 to 12 (quick-eye mean, then quick questions), explore at the computer 12 to 26 (class data in a Scratch list), mini-lesson 26 to 37.5 (click to reveal each step and answer; the mean program with a trace table), brain break 37.5 to 43, worksheet 43 to 75.5 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 75.5 to 77 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 77 to 82, exit slip 82 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. Before the lesson: make the starter project (one sprite, an empty list called data) and share its link, or let children build it from the code slide.

p6l9-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: 4 each. Total 16 stickers, shared between 4 friends. (This is the “fair share” idea behind the mean.) Puzzle 2: No: four of the five friends have $4 or less. One very large amount pulls the equal share up. The middle value ($3) says more about a typical friend. Guesses are welcome. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l9-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9.5. Quick-eye mean. Hide the slide (or cover the numbers), show one round for 5 seconds, then hide it again. Children write a guess on paper (no points, no ranking). Click to show the mean and ask how they guessed. Two rounds only. Round 1: 8 + 12 + 10 + 9 + 11 = 50, 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Round 2: 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 37 = 55, 55 ÷ 5 = 11. Ask after round 2: "Most of you guessed about 5. Why is the mean 11?" (The 37 pulls the mean up: we come back to this today.) Ask: "How did you guess so fast?" Listen for: pick a middle number, then check the big ones and small ones balance.

p6l9-warm2.note: Minutes 9.5 to 12. Three questions only. Read each aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show. Answers: 1) 6 (18 ÷ 3). 2) 60 (5 × 12: we can turn the mean back into a total). 3) 22.4 (112 ÷ 5): four of the five values are 3, yet the mean is over 20. Ask on 2: "How did you get a total from a mean?" This is the key move for today’s missing-value puzzles.

p6l9-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 26 (this slide 12 to 16.5). Everyone types the number of letters in their full name (no spaces) in the chat; copy the list onto the slide or a shared board. Each child estimates the mean, then works it out by hand (total ÷ how many). Scratch is NOT opened in this part: the list-and-loop program is built once, live, in the mean program slide of the mini-lesson, so nothing is built twice. Then the prediction: "Our tutor joins with a 30-letter name. Will the mean go up a little or a lot?" Add 30 to the list and work out the new mean by hand. Watch for children who divide by the wrong count or who add a value twice. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if you add a very small value, 1, to the list instead of 30? Predict: does the mean go up or down? Does the median change? Test it and explain. Answer: The mean goes down (1 is below the other values, which are name lengths of about 8 or more). The median moves only to the next value along, so it changes by much less than the mean. One extreme value pulls the mean more than the median.

p6l9-explore2.note: Minutes 16.5 to 26. Two questions only. Let pairs keep testing (add other values: which new value keeps the mean exactly the same?), then gather to answer. Answers: 1) Pick a value in the middle, then check that the values above it and below it roughly balance. 2) It went up, a lot, because 30 is far above every other value. One big value pulls the mean towards it. Finisher answer: adding a value equal to the mean keeps the mean the same (it is already "level").

p6l9-teach1.note: Minutes 26 to 27.5. Teach. Build the towers with real cubes on camera if you can. Think-aloud: "The 9-tower gives 3 cubes to the 3-tower; the 7-tower gives 1 cube to the 5-tower. Now they are all 6. That level is the mean." Click: the levelled towers, the total, then the mean. Say: "Levelling out and total ÷ how many give the same answer, because moving cubes keeps the total and sharing it equally is exactly dividing by how many towers." Ask: "Could the level ever be above the tallest tower?" (No: we only move cubes downhill.)

p6l9-we1.note: Minutes 27.5 to 29.5. Click to reveal each step. Think-aloud: “Goals in 5 matches: 3, 0, 4, 1, 2. The 0 is a real value: that match counts. Total 3 + 0 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 10. Five matches, so the mean is 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Check by balancing: 3 is 1 above, 4 is 2 above: 3 above in all. 0 is 2 below, 1 is 1 below: 3 below in all. They balance, so 2 is right.” Why the check works: levelling moves the extra cubes above the mean into the gaps below it, so "how much above" must equal "how much below". Common mistake: dividing by 4 because 0 "is nothing" (10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 is wrong).

p6l9-code1.note:
Minutes 29.5 to 32.5. This is the ONLY place the mean program is built. Pre-build the project with the list data already holding 3, 0, 4, 1, 2 so the live demo takes about 150 seconds: show the blocks, run it, children copy the blocks (Variables: total and i; the list data). Then trace it on the slide: click to add each row. Think-aloud: "i starts at 1, so item 1 of data is 3: total becomes 3. Change i by 1. Item 2 is 0: total stays 3. Item 3 is 4: total 7. Item 4 is 1: total 8. Item 5 is 2: total 10. The loop ran length of data = 5 times. 10 ÷ 5 = 2." Why "length of data" and not 5? Then the program still works when the list grows (teaching slide before page 2). Python version (optional, for children who know Python):
data = [3, 0, 4, 1, 2] # goals in 5 matches
total = 0
for value in data:
 total = total + value
mean = total / len(data)
print("Total:", total)
print("Mean:", mean)
above = 0
for value in data:
 if value > mean:
 above = above + 1
print("Above the mean:", above)
It prints: Total: 10, Mean: 2.0 (Python writes 2 as 2.0 after a division), Above the mean: 2.

p6l9-try1.note: Minutes 32.5 to 34. Whiteboards. a) 45 ÷ 5 = 9 (evenly spaced: the middle value). b) 20 ÷ 4 = 5: not one of the values; check −3, −1, −1, +5 balances. c) 15 ÷ 5 = 3: both zeros count. Anyone who wrote 5 for c divided by 3 values; anyone who wrote 4 for b found the middle, not the mean.

p6l9-we2.note: Minutes 34 to 36. Click each step. Think-aloud: “The mean of 4 test scores is 15, so the total must be 4 × 15 = 60. The three I know make 12 + 18 + 14 = 44. The missing score is 60 − 44 = 16. I never subtract from the mean: I subtract from the total.” The last box: a new value equal to the mean changes nothing (5 × 15 = 75 = 60 + 15). Common mistake: 15 − 12 − 18 … (subtracting from the mean). Ask: "What number do we take the known values away FROM?" (the total).

p6l9-key.note: Minutes 36 to 37.5. What changes the mean (folded in from the old change slide; use data 2, 4, 6, mean 4, and predict with thumbs): a value of 4 keeps it the same (16 ÷ 4 = 4); add 1 to every value: 3, 5, 7 gives 5; remove the 6: 2, 4 gives 3; change the 6 to 18: 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Worksheet Q3 is like this. Say the key idea together: "Mean = total ÷ how many. Total = mean × how many." Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Dividing by the wrong count: leaving out a value of 0, or forgetting the new value when one is added. (2) Finding a missing value from the MEAN instead of from the TOTAL (mean × how many) minus the known values. (3) Thinking the mean must be one of the values, or that it is always a typical value even when one value is extreme.

p6l9-break.note: Minutes 37.5 to 43. 5.5 minutes. Use any online dice roller. After 3 rounds, add the three totals and divide by 3 together (the answer may be a decimal: that is fine). Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p6l9-teachmed.note: Minutes 43 to 45. Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q4). Think-aloud: “Goals by 7 players: 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 25. The mean is 42 ÷ 7 = 6, but 6 of the 7 players scored fewer than 6! The one big value pulled the mean up. The median, the middle value in order, is 3. That describes a typical player better.” Ask: "If the 25 became 250, what happens to the mean? To the median?" (Mean (17 + 250) ÷ 7 is about 38; the median is still 3.) Point out: for an even number of values the median is halfway between the middle two (we will not need that today). The mode is useful for things like shoe sizes: the shop wants the most common size.

p6l9-ws1.note: Minutes 45 to 60. Walk around (or visit breakout rooms). Ask "What is the total? How many values?" and "Predict before you calculate." In Q3 insist on a prediction in words before the number.

p6l9-ws1ans.note: Minutes 60 to 63. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q2 (the missing value from the total), about 35 seconds a question. Q2: 17 × 4 = 68; 68 − 15 − 20 − 14 = 19; for a mean of 18 over 5 games the total must be 90, so 90 − 68 = 22. Q3: a) 60 ÷ 6 = 10; b) every value up 3; c) 36 ÷ 4 = 9; d) the total goes up by 30, shared by 5: up 6, so 16. Q4: 154 ÷ 7 = 22; in order the 4th value is $15; $12 appears twice; only the $69 pupil gets more than $22.

p6l9-teachany.note: Minutes 63 to 65.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 asks which blocks must change). Think-aloud: "A number typed into the code is fixed. When the list grows, the program does not know. length of data is always the right count, so the loop visits every item and we divide by the right number." Try it live: add 8 to the list and run both versions.

p6l9-ws2.note: Minutes 65.5 to 72.5. Children work alone on Q5; Q6 (temperatures, plan the code) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook, and children who finish Q5 may build it in Scratch with the temperatures in a list called temps. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Python fans use the box on the page. Note who needs a short catch-up.

p6l9-ws2ans.note: Minutes 72.5 to 75.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q5 (why the code must use length of scores). Q6 is the take-home question: its answer is here so children can mark it at home, and you take it up at the start of the next lesson (the if compares item i of temps with mean; if the counter is set inside the loop it resets every time). Q5: i goes 1, 2, 3, 4 and item i is 5, 9, 6, 12; 32 ÷ 4 = 8; with 13 added the total is 45 and the length is 5, so 9. Q6: 29 + 31 + 33 + 30 + 32 + 34 + 28 = 217, 217 ÷ 7 = 31; hotter than 31: 33, 32 and 34. The if compares item i of temps with mean, and change count by 1 counts it.

p6l9-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Answers: 1) 7 (6 × 7 = 42; 3 + 5 + 8 + 9 + 10 = 35; 42 − 35 = 7). 2) Two sets: 1, 3, 11 and 2, 3, 10 (total 15; the middle is 3; the smallest is 1 or 2, so the largest is 15 − 3 − 1 = 11 or 15 − 3 − 2 = 10). 3) 73 (30 × 70 = 2100; 10 × 64 = 640; 2100 − 640 = 1460; 1460 ÷ 20 = 73). Test any of them in code: put the numbers in a list and run the mean program.

p6l9-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use as a pair challenge or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. More are in the question bank. Answers: 1) (a) 12 (5 × 8 = 40, 4 × 7 = 28, 40 − 28 = 12). (b) No. Removing a number above the mean (like 12) lowers the mean, but removing a number below the mean raises it. Example: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 has mean 8; remove 4 and 6, 8, 10, 12 has mean 9. 2) (a) 50 (10 × 32 = 320, 9 × 30 = 270, 320 − 270 = 50). (b) 33: 270 + 60 = 330 and 330 ÷ 10 = 33.

p6l9-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried the Challenge, or if they are stuck. The diagrams show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Which totals can you find? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p6l9-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried, with the "see it" slide. The big idea in both: work with TOTALS, not means. Q2 also has a levelling explanation: the 10th score must bring itself up to 32 and also give 2 extra to each of the 9 earlier games. Q1(b): Ali is wrong. Removing a number ABOVE the mean (like 12) lowers the mean; removing one BELOW the mean raises it. Example: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 has mean 8; remove 4 and the mean of 6, 8, 10, 12 is 9. Check for (a): 28 + 12 = 40 and 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Q2(b): the best she can do is 60 in game 10, so the total is 270 + 60 = 330 and the mean is 33. Test either in Scratch: put the numbers in a list and run the mean program.

p6l9-talk.note: Minutes 77 to 82. One question only. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then volunteers share. Second question (only if flex is left; otherwise the opener of the next lesson): “Can the mean be bigger than every value in the list? Why or why not?” (Only if flex is left; otherwise it is the opener of the next lesson.) Answer: Yes: the mean of 2 and 3 is 2.5, a number nobody in the group has. No: the mean is always between the smallest and the largest value. Levelling out moves cubes from taller towers to shorter ones, so the level can never be higher than the tallest tower or lower than the shortest. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

p6l9-exit.note: Minutes 82 to 86. Answer: 10 (total 3 × 9 = 27; 27 − 5 − 12 = 10). New mean 10 (27 + 13 = 40, 40 ÷ 4 = 10). “Today you found means by levelling and by dividing, worked backwards from a mean to a total, and caught a misleading average. And your code added up a whole list for you. Next lesson is our Showcase Challenge: start thinking about a puzzle you would like to turn into a program.” Homework thought for next lesson: decide which starter you will change (A, B, C or Clock Jumper) and what your twist will be, so you can start building straight away. Extension: Make a list of 5 whole numbers with mean 10, median 8 and mode 7 (one answer: 7, 7, 8, 13, 15). Then change your program so it also finds the largest value in the list.

p6l9-reflect.note: Minutes 86 to 88. Looking back is 2 full minutes, after the exit slip, and is never shortened. Everyone has the box: it is on the Finish page, a page every child reaches. Say: "Two minutes, just for you. Finish: something I did well, the hardest part was, and tick what helped. You can write pass. If you are still stuck, tick that box and I will check in with you in the open session, in the shared room, with your parent nearby." Never collect it in front of the group and never read an answer out. Never ask a child to show the box to the camera; a child who ticks “I am still stuck” is followed up after class through the parent. Praise the strategy, not the speed: say "you re-ordered the numbers, and that is what got you unstuck", never "you were quick". If a child ticks I am still stuck, check in during the open session the same day: visit the shared breakout room or use a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never by private message. If a child writes "everything" or "I am bad at maths", say quietly in the open session: "Thank you for telling me. Let's find one small thing that worked today," and point to a specific item they got right. If a child writes that nothing was hard, ask what would make it harder.
